claim: Cdc48/p97 and its adaptors Ufd1-Npl4 participate in ribosome-associated degradation (RAD) by mediating the clearance of ubiquitinated, tRNA-linked nascent peptides from ribosomes.
source: Here we show that the ubiquitin (Ub) pathway segregase Cdc48/p97 and its adaptors Ufd1-Npl4 participate in ribosome-associated degradation (RAD) by mediating the clearance of ubiquitinated, tRNA-linked nascent peptides from ribosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data presented in the manuscript, including puromycin release assays, UBA bead capture, and pulse-chase experiments showing accumulation of ubiquitinated nascent peptides on ribosomes in cdc48 mutants.

claim: Budding yeast Cdc48 functions downstream of the Ub ligases Ltn1 and Ubr1 to release nascent proteins from the ribosome so that they can be degraded by the proteasome.
source: Through characterization of both endogenously-generated and heterologous model substrates for the RAD pathway, we conclude that budding yeast Cdc48 functions downstream of the Ub ligases Ltn1 and Ubr1 to release nascent proteins from the ribosome so that they can be degraded by the proteasome.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that deletion of LTN1 or UBR1 decreases accumulation of tUNPs on cdc48-3 ribosomes (Figure 3A), and that ubiquitinated forms of non-stop reporters accumulate in ufd1 mutants but not in ltn1Δ mutants (Figure 3D).

claim: Defective RAD could contribute to the pathophysiology of human diseases caused by mutations in p97.
source: Defective RAD could contribute to the pathophysiology of human diseases caused by mutations in p97.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the established role of p97 in RAD and known associations between p97 mutations and human diseases.

claim: Low concentrations of hygromycin B and paromomycin inhibited growth of multiple cdc48 mutants and the adaptor mutants npl4-1, ufd1, ubx1Δ, and ubx2Δ.
source: However, low concentrations of hygromycin B and paromomycin inhibited growth of multiple cdc48 mutants and the adaptor mutants npl4-1, ufd1, ubx1Δ, and ubx2Δ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B demonstrating growth inhibition of these mutants on plates containing hygromycin B and paromomycin.

claim: Hygromycin B and paromomycin belong to the aminoglycoside class of antibiotics that bind close to the decoding center and affect translational fidelity.
source: Hygromycin B and paromomycin belong to the aminoglycoside class of antibiotics that bind close to the decoding center and affect translational fidelity (Carter et al., 2000; Kim and Craig, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Deletion of LTN1 leads to hygromycin-sensitivity.
source: Deletion of LTN1 leads to hygromycin-sensitivity and since Ltn1 is involved in QC of NSD pathway substrates (Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010), we explored the possibility that Cdc48–Ufd1–Npl4 and one or more Ubx proteins also function in this pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010.

claim: Ltn1 is involved in QC of NSD pathway substrates.
source: Deletion of LTN1 leads to hygromycin-sensitivity and since Ltn1 is involved in QC of NSD pathway substrates (Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010), we explored the possibility that Cdc48–Ufd1–Npl4 and one or more Ubx proteins also function in this pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010.

claim: Cdc48 activity is not required for ribosome assembly.
source: Coomassie blue staining of purified ribosomes confirmed that Cdc48 activity was not required for their assembly (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, lane 3), a conclusion that was further validated by sucrose gradient fractionation of ribosomes from wildtype, cdc48-3, and ufd1-2 whole cell lysates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Coomassie blue staining data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) and sucrose gradient fractionation data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Ub conjugates accumulate on ribosomes affinity-purified from cdc48-3 cells.
source: Immunoblotting for Ub revealed strong accumulation of Ub conjugates on ribosomes affinity-purified from cdc48-3 cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Ub conjugates accumulate on ribosomes isolated from cdc48-3 and npl4-1 mutants by pelleting through a sucrose cushion.
source: Again, Ub conjugates were observed to accumulate on ribosomes in cdc48-3 and npl4-1 mutants (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Conjugate accumulation on cdc48-3 and npl4-1 ribosomes exceeded that observed for ribosomes isolated from cells treated with the proteasome inhibitor MG132.
source: Additionally, conjugate accumulation on cdc48-3 and npl4-1 ribosomes exceeded that observed for ribosomes isolated from cells treated with the proteasome inhibitor MG132, a result that will be further discussed below.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of immunoblotting data in Figure 1B.

claim: The ATPase activity of Cdc48 is required to prevent accumulation of ribosome-associated Ub conjugates.
source: To determine whether the ATPase activity of Cdc48 was required to prevent accumulation of ribosome-associated Ub conjugates, ribosomes were pelleted from cdc48-3 mutant cells expressing plasmid-borne wildtype CDC48, or a mutant (Q2) deficient in ATPase activity (Ye et al., 2003). Whereas CDC48 complemented the cdc48-3 phenotype, high levels of Ub conjugates were detected on ribosomes isolated from cells expressing the cdc48-Q2 mutant (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C comparing wildtype CDC48 and the ATPase-deficient Q2 mutant.

claim: Both Cdc48 and Ufd1 cofractionate with affinity-purified ribosomes isolated under stringent conditions.
source: Consistent with the idea that Cdc48 ATPase functions at the ribosome to mediate release of ubiquitinated nascent peptides, both Cdc48 and Ufd1 were found to cofractionate with affinity-purified ribosomes isolated under stringent conditions (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Puromycin treatment of ribosomes from cdc48-3 but not wildtype cells released ubiquitinated proteins that were enriched on the UBA resin.
source: Puromycin treatment of ribosomes from cdc48-3 but not wildtype cells released ubiquitinated proteins that were enriched on the UBA resin (Figure 2A, top panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A similar result was obtained with ribosomes isolated from npl4-1 and ufd1-1 mutants.
source: A similar result was obtained with ribosomes isolated from npl4-1 and ufd1-1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The conjugates observed in Figure 2A were linked to puromycin because they cross-reacted with an antibody specific for puromycin.
source: The conjugates observed in Figure 2A were indeed linked to puromycin because they cross-reacted with an antibody specific for puromycin (Figure 2A, bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data with anti-puromycin antibody shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The same was true for Ub conjugates released from npl4-1 and ufd1-2 ribosomes.
source: The same was true for Ub conjugates released from npl4-1 and ufd1-2 ribosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No Ub immunoreactivity was recovered from mutant ribosomes in the absence of puromycin treatment.
source: The fact that no Ub immunoreactivity was recovered from mutant ribosomes in the absence of puromycin treatment validated our assumption that the UBA resin largely excluded mega-complexes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental design and results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At least some of the Ub conjugates that accumulated on cdc48 and npl4 ribosomes must be ubiquitinated nascent proteins linked to tRNA.
source: This experiment also suggests that at least some of the Ub conjugates that accumulated on cdc48 and npl4 ribosomes (Figure 1A,B) must be ubiquitinated nascent proteins linked to tRNA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the puromycin release experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Transfer of Ub conjugates to puromycin was RNAse A-sensitive.
source: Immunoblotting for Ub revealed that both the control and RNAse-treated ribosomes contained Ub conjugates that bound the UBA beads (Figure 2B, top panel, lanes 2 and 3). However, ribosomes pre-treated with RNAse no longer yielded puromycin-reactive conjugates (Figure 2B, bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B comparing RNAse-treated and untreated samples.

claim: Pre-treating lysate with RNAse before affinity purification of ribosomes eliminated recovery of both Ub-, and puromycin immunoreactivity.
source: By contrast, pre-treating lysate with RNAse before affinity purification of ribosomes eliminated recovery of both Ub-, and puromycin immunoreactivity (Figure 2B, lane 4, top and bottom panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, lane 4.

claim: Ub conjugates were precipitated from cdc48-3 ribosomes by CTAB in an RNAse-sensitive manner.
source: In parallel with results obtained previously using puromycin, Ub conjugates were precipitated from cdc48-3 ribosomes in an RNAse-sensitive manner (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by CTAB precipitation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ribosomes from both cdc48-3 and ufd1-2 cells contained far higher levels of radiolabeled high MW Ub conjugates than wildtype ribosomes.
source: Strikingly, ribosomes from both cdc48-3 and ufd1-2 cells contained far higher levels of radiolabeled high MW Ub conjugates than wildtype ribosomes, and a substantial portion of this signal persisted on ribosomes for 10–20 min (Figure 2D), which is considerably longer than the time required to synthesize a protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The low signal on wildtype ribosomes was not due to inefficient incorporation.
source: Importantly, the low signal on wildtype ribosomes was not due to inefficient incorporation, because the WT inputs for the UBA fractionation step actually contained slightly more total pulse-labeled species (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Cdc48 and its cofactors Ufd1 and Npl4 prevent accumulation of ubiquitinated, tRNA-linked nascent chains on the ribosome.
source: Taken together, the experiments described thus far indicate that Cdc48 and its cofactors Ufd1 and Npl4 prevent accumulation of ubiquitinated, tRNA-linked nascent chains on the ribosome.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on multiple experiments including puromycin release, CTAB precipitation, and pulse-chase experiments.

claim: Other Cdc48 cofactors including Ubx2, Ubx4, Ubx6, and Ufd2 did not appear to contribute to clearance of tUNPs from the ribosome.
source: Notably, other Cdc48 cofactors including Ubx2, Ubx4, Ubx6, and Ufd2 did not appear to contribute to clearance of tUNPs from the ribosome (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Additional loss of LTN1 or UBR1 resulted in a marked decrease in the level of tUNPs on cdc48-3 ribosomes.
source: The data in Figure 3A demonstrate that additional loss of LTN1 or UBR1 resulted in a marked decrease in the level of tUNPs on cdc48-3 ribosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: GFHNS accumulated maximally in ufd1 mutants (similar to levels observed for ltn1Δ), and also exhibited significant accumulation in npl4-1 and cdc48-3.
source: Amongst the Cdc48 pathway mutants examined, GFHNS accumulated maximally in ufd1 mutants (similar to levels observed for ltn1Δ), and also exhibited significant accumulation in npl4-1 and cdc48-3 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Accumulation of GFHNS in ufd1-2 cells resulted from stabilization of the non-stop reporter.
source: Cycloheximide chase analysis in ufd1-2 cells indicated that accumulation resulted from stabilization of the non-stop reporter (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The same reporter containing a stop codon was not degraded and accumulated at a much higher level than the NS reporter.
source: As observed in earlier studies (Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010), the same reporter containing a stop codon was not degraded and accumulated at a much higher level than the NS reporter (Figure 3C; amounts loaded were adjusted to yield signals of equal intensity at 0 min).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 3C and citation to prior work.

claim: GFHNS accumulated in an ubiquitinated form in ufd1-1 and ufd1-2 but not in ltn1Δ mutants.
source: Immunoblotting for Ub demonstrated that GFHNS accumulated in an ubiquitinated form in ufd1-1 and ufd1-2 but not in ltn1Δ mutants (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both Cdc48 and Ufd1 were co-immunoprecipitated with GFHNS, but not GFHStop, even though GFHStop was more abundant.
source: The role of the Cdc48 complex in reporter degradation appeared to be direct, because both Cdc48 and Ufd1 were co-immunoprecipitated with GFHNS, but not GFHStop, even though GFHStop was more abundant (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: GFHNS accumulates on 80S ribosomes in ltn1Δ mutants.
source: GFHNS accumulates on 80S ribosomes in ltn1Δ mutants (Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010.

claim: An RNAse-sensitive species of GFHNS was detected on ribosomes from ltn1Δ, as well as those from cdc48-3 and ufd1-2 mutants, but not from wildtype cells.
source: Strikingly, immunoblotting revealed an RNAse-sensitive species on ribosomes from ltn1Δ, as well as those from cdc48-3 and ufd1-2 mutants, but not from wildtype cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fraction of GFHNS linked to tRNA was low.
source: The fraction of GFHNS linked to tRNA was low. It is not clear whether this was due to hydrolysis of the tRNA linkage in vivo or in vitro.
evidence: The claim is based on observation of data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and represents speculation about the cause.

claim: Levels of tRNA-linked PrANS in cdc48-3 and ltn1Δ cell lysates were equivalent to those detected in dom34Δ and ski7Δ.
source: Interestingly, levels of tRNA-linked PrANS in cdc48-3 and ltn1Δ cell lysates were equivalent to those detected in dom34Δ and ski7Δ, bona fide components of the NSD pathway (Figure 4A; equivalent loading confirmed by staining with Ponceau S and immunoblotting for tubulin, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The RNAse-sensitive species of PrANS peaked in the 80S fractions isolated from ltn1Δ mutants but was found in both the 60S and 80S-containing fractions from cdc48-3 cells.
source: Immunoblotting for PrANS revealed that the RNAse-sensitive species peaked in the 80S fractions isolated from ltn1Δ mutants but was found in both the 60S and 80S-containing fractions from cdc48-3 cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sucrose gradient fractionation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Modified forms of slower mobility than the tRNA-linked species were detected in 60S ribosomes from cdc48-3 but not ltn1Δ, suggesting that these high MW species are Ltn1-dependent Ub conjugates.
source: Additionally, modified forms of slower mobility than the tRNA-linked species were detected in 60S ribosomes from cdc48-3 but not ltn1Δ, suggesting that these high MW species are Ltn1-dependent Ub conjugates.
evidence: The claim is based on observation of data in Figure 4B and represents an inference about the nature of the high MW species.

claim: Only a small fraction of the PrANS detected on ribosomes migrated as Ub-conjugated species.
source: Only a small fraction of the PrANS detected on ribosomes migrated as Ub-conjugated species. This is consistent with what is typically observed for most Ub-dependent substrates upon inhibition of their degradation, and presumably reflects robust cytosolic deubiquitination activity.
evidence: The claim is based on observation of data and comparison to typical behavior of Ub-dependent substrates.

claim: Overproduction of PrANS from the GAL promoter may overwhelm Ltn1, which is inabundant.
source: In addition, overproduction of PrANS from the GAL promoter may overwhelm Ltn1, which is inabundant (Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about why only a small fraction of PrANS is ubiquitinated, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Ribosomes isolated from cells with inhibited proteasomes contained far less tUNPs than ribosomes from cdc48-3 and npl4-1 cells.
source: Ribosomes isolated from cells with inhibited proteasomes contained far less tUNPs than ribosomes from cdc48-3 and npl4-1 cells (Figure 5A; the input lysates and ribosome pellets for this experiment are shown in Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by UBA bead capture data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: This result is in striking contrast to what we previously reported for proteasomes isolated from cdc48-3 and MG132-treated cells—both contained very high levels of accumulated Ub conjugates.
source: This result is in striking contrast to what we previously reported for proteasomes isolated from cdc48-3 and MG132-treated cells—both contained very high levels of accumulated Ub conjugates (Verma et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim compares current results to prior published work by the authors.

claim: A similar result was obtained using the cim3-1 mutant instead of MG132 treatment.
source: A similar result was obtained using the cim3-1 mutant instead of MG132 treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; cim3-1 is a ts allele of the gene that encodes the proteasome subunit Rpt6).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Whereas most of the PrANS fractionated in the ribosome pellet in cdc48-3 cells (a substantial portion of which remained linked to tRNA), the opposite was true in cim3-1 cells, where the bulk of the PrANS was recovered in the supernatant fraction.
source: Notably, whereas most of the PrANS fractionated in the ribosome pellet in cdc48-3 cells (a substantial portion of which remained linked to tRNA), the opposite was true in cim3-1 cells, where the bulk of the PrANS was recovered in the supernatant fraction (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The proportion of PrANS that accumulated as full length or truncated species in vivo and its susceptibility to proteolytic clipping in native cell extract differed for cdc48-3 and cim3-1 mutants.
source: Comparison of extracts made by lysing cells directly in SDS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) or under native conditions (Figure 5B) revealed that the proportion of PrANS that accumulated as full length or truncated species in vivo and its susceptibility to proteolytic clipping in native cell extract differed for cdc48-3 and cim3-1 mutants.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: cdc48-3 and ufd1-2 mutations stabilized Gnd1PTC, but ltn1Δ was without effect.
source: The data in Figure 6A confirmed stabilization of Gnd1PTC in ubr1Δ. Notably, cdc48-3 and ufd1-2 mutations also stabilized Gnd1PTC, but ltn1Δ was without effect (equivalent loading confirmed in Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Gnd1PTC was also stabilized in upf1Δ.
source: Gnd1PTC was also stabilized in upf1Δ.
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Upf1 is a RING domain Ub ligase that plays a crucial role in NMD and stimulates the degradation of aberrant PTC translation products.
source: Upf1 is a RING domain Ub ligase (Takahashi et al., 2008) that plays a crucial role in NMD and stimulates the degradation of aberrant PTC translation products (Kuroha et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: An RNAse-sensitive species of Gnd1PTC was found on ribosomes from cdc48-3 mutants as well as ufd1-2, ubr1Δ and upf1Δ mutants, but not from wildtype cells.
source: Fractionation of lysates prepared in an identical manner revealed an RNAse-sensitive species on ribosomes but not in post-ribosomal supernatants isolated from cdc48-3 mutants (Figure 6C) as well as ufd1-2, ubr1Δ and upf1Δ mutants (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Little tRNA-linked Gnd1PTC was found in dom34Δ mutants.
source: In contrast, little tRNA-linked substrate was found in dom34Δ mutants (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The tRNA-linked species of Gnd1PTC was not detected on ribosomes from ltn1Δ.
source: Strikingly, the tRNA-linked species was not detected on ribosomes from ltn1Δ (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observation mentioned in the text.

claim: Cdc48–Ufd1–Npl4 acts downstream of Ltn1 to promote release of the non-stop peptide from the ribosome, so that it can be degraded by the proteasome.
source: Our data suggest that Cdc48–Ufd1–Npl4 acts downstream of Ltn1 to promote release of the non-stop peptide from the ribosome, so that it can be degraded by the proteasome.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: How Ltn1 and the Cdc48 complex promotes release of nascent peptides from the ribosome remains unknown.
source: How Ltn1 and the Cdc48 complex does this remains unknown.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the limits of current knowledge.

claim: This remains unknown for any NSD or NGD pathway substrate.
source: Indeed, this remains unknown for any NSD or NGD pathway substrate; the Dom34-Hbs1 complex lacks the residues necessary for hydrolysis of the peptidyl-tRNA bond, and the two budding yeast peptidyl-tRNA hydrolases, Pth1 and Pth2, are non-essential mitochondrial proteins whose transmembrane configurations are currently unknown (Rosas-Sandoval et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work and represents established knowledge about the field.

claim: The Dom34-Hbs1 complex lacks the residues necessary for hydrolysis of the peptidyl-tRNA bond.
source: Indeed, this remains unknown for any NSD or NGD pathway substrate; the Dom34-Hbs1 complex lacks the residues necessary for hydrolysis of the peptidyl-tRNA bond, and the two budding yeast peptidyl-tRNA hydrolases, Pth1 and Pth2, are non-essential mitochondrial proteins whose transmembrane configurations are currently unknown (Rosas-Sandoval et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about the Dom34-Hbs1 complex.

claim: The two budding yeast peptidyl-tRNA hydrolases, Pth1 and Pth2, are non-essential mitochondrial proteins whose transmembrane configurations are currently unknown.
source: Indeed, this remains unknown for any NSD or NGD pathway substrate; the Dom34-Hbs1 complex lacks the residues necessary for hydrolysis of the peptidyl-tRNA bond, and the two budding yeast peptidyl-tRNA hydrolases, Pth1 and Pth2, are non-essential mitochondrial proteins whose transmembrane configurations are currently unknown (Rosas-Sandoval et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Rosas-Sandoval et al., 2002.

claim: Direct physical association of Cdc48 and Ufd1 with both affinity-purified ribosomes and the NSD pathway substrate GFHNS was observed.
source: We observed direct physical association of Cdc48 and Ufd1 with both affinity-purified ribosomes and the NSD pathway substrate GFHNS.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figures 1D and 3E.

claim: This interaction was highly specific, because Cdc48 and Ufd1 did not bind the same substrate when it was translated from a message that includes a stop codon.
source: This interaction was highly specific, because Cdc48 and Ufd1 did not bind the same substrate when it was translated from a message that includes a stop codon.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Cdc48, Ufd1, and Npl4 are components of the newly identified Ribosome Quality Control (RQC) complex, which also contains Ltn1, Rqc1 and Tae2 and associates with the 60S ribosomal subunit.
source: While this manuscript was in revision, it was reported that Cdc48, Ufd1, and Npl4 are components of the newly identified Ribosome Quality Control (RQC) complex, which also contains Ltn1, Rqc1 and Tae2 and associates with the 60S ribosomal subunit. The latter two proteins, like Ltn1 and Cdc48–Ufd1–Npl4, are highly conserved and have mammalian homologs (Brandman et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to work by Brandman et al., 2012.

claim: Both Ltn1 and Rqc1 help link Cdc48–Ufd1–Npl4 to RQC.
source: Both Ltn1 and Rqc1 help link Cdc48–Ufd1–Npl4 to RQC.
evidence: The claim is based on information from the cited work by Brandman et al., 2012.

claim: Rqc1 associates with and is required for the degradation of an Ltn1 substrate that contains an internal polyarginine sequence.
source: Rqc1 associates with and is required for the degradation of an Ltn1 substrate that contains an internal polyarginine sequence, but a functional role for Cdc48–Ufd1–Npl4 in RQC was not established by Brandman et al. (2012).
evidence: The claim is based on information from the cited work by Brandman et al., 2012.

claim: A functional role for Cdc48–Ufd1–Npl4 in RQC was not established by Brandman et al. (2012).
source: Rqc1 associates with and is required for the degradation of an Ltn1 substrate that contains an internal polyarginine sequence, but a functional role for Cdc48–Ufd1–Npl4 in RQC was not established by Brandman et al. (2012).
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the cited work by Brandman et al., 2012.

claim: Ltn1 and RQC are reported to be predominantly bound to 60S ribosomal subunits, suggesting that they may act downstream of the initial recognition and splitting of a stalled ribosome.
source: Ltn1 (Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010) and RQC (Brandman et al., 2012) are reported to be predominantly bound to 60S ribosomal subunits, suggesting that they may act downstream of the initial recognition and splitting of a stalled ribosome.
evidence: The claim is based on citations to prior work and represents an inference about the timing of Ltn1/RQC action.

claim: In ltn1Δ cells, GFHNS accumulates on 80S monosomes.
source: However, in ltn1Δ cells, GFHNS accumulates on 80S monosomes (Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010.

claim: tRNA-linked PrANS appeared to be concentrated in monosomes in ltn1Δ.
source: Likewise, we report here that tRNA-linked PrANS appeared to be concentrated in monosomes in ltn1Δ.
evidence: The claim is supported by sucrose gradient fractionation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: tRNA-linked PrANS was spread more broadly across 60S and 80S fractions in extracts from cdc48-3 cells.
source: By contrast, tRNA-linked PrANS was spread more broadly across 60S and 80S fractions in extracts from cdc48-3 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by sucrose gradient fractionation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The different fractionation behavior of tRNA-linked PrANS in ltn1Δ and cdc48 mutants may reflect leakiness of the cdc48 mutation or Cdc48-independent ribosome splitting.
source: The different fractionation behavior of tRNA-linked PrANS in ltn1Δ and cdc48 mutants may reflect leakiness of the cdc48 mutation (the experiment was done at the semi-permissive temperature of 30°C) or Cdc48-independent ribosome splitting.
evidence: The claim represents speculation about the cause of observed differences in fractionation behavior.

claim: Extensive accumulation of endogenous, tRNA-linked ubiquitinated nascent polypeptides (tUNPs) on ribosomes was observed in Cdc48 pathway mutants.
source: In addition to observing accumulation of engineered NSD pathway reporter proteins in Cdc48 pathway mutants, we also observed extensive accumulation of endogenous, tRNA-linked ubiquitinated nascent polypeptides (tUNPs) on ribosomes in these cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data including puromycin release and UBA bead capture experiments shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: These tUNPs could potentially arise from multiple sources including misfolded domains, mRNAs whose transcription was prematurely terminated, mRNAs or nascent peptides containing sequences that cause ribosome pausing, or mRNAs that encode premature termination codons.
source: These tUNPs could potentially arise from multiple sources including misfolded domains (Turner and Varshavsky, 2000), mRNAs whose transcription was prematurely terminated, mRNAs or nascent peptides containing sequences that cause ribosome pausing (Ingolia et al., 2011) or mRNAs that encode premature termination codons (e.g., Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about potential sources of tUNPs, supported by citations and reference to data.

claim: At least two Ub ligases (Ltn1 and Ubr1) contributed to accumulation of tUNPs.
source: Thus it is perhaps not surprising that at least two Ub ligases (Ltn1 and Ubr1) contributed to their accumulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating that deletion of LTN1 or UBR1 decreases tUNP accumulation.

claim: It is unlikely that there is a single pathway or mechanism for disposing of tUNPs.
source: In any event, we believe it is unlikely that there is a single pathway or mechanism for disposing of tUNPs.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the complexity of potential tUNP sources.

claim: Stalls in translation elongation lead to endonucleolytic cleavage of the mRNA upstream of the 3′-most ribosome.
source: Because stalls in translation elongation lead to endonucleolytic cleavage of the mRNA upstream of the 3′-most ribosome (Tsuboi et al., 2012), each trailing ribosome will present a unique substrate to the UPS, and may be processed by a different mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to work by Tsuboi et al., 2012.

claim: The translasome is a supercomplex defined by mass spectrometric analysis of the translation initiation factor eIF3 and found to contain both ribosome and proteasome subunits as well as chaperones involved in protein QC.
source: The intimacy with which protein biosynthesis is coupled to protein degradation is highlighted by the identification of the translasome, a supercomplex defined by mass spectrometric analysis of the translation initiation factor eIF3 and found to contain both ribosome and proteasome subunits as well as chaperones involved in protein QC (Sha et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to work by Sha et al., 2009.

claim: Homozygous lister mice deficient in Listerin (Ltn1) function exhibit severe neurological dysfunction.
source: Indeed, homozygous lister mice deficient in Listerin (Ltn1) function exhibit severe neurological dysfunction (Chu et al., 2009), whereas mutations in human Ubr1 result in the Johanson–Blizzard syndrome characterized by, amongst other phenotypes, frequent mental retardation (Hwang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to work by Chu et al., 2009.

claim: Mutations in human Ubr1 result in the Johanson–Blizzard syndrome characterized by, amongst other phenotypes, frequent mental retardation.
source: Indeed, homozygous lister mice deficient in Listerin (Ltn1) function exhibit severe neurological dysfunction (Chu et al., 2009), whereas mutations in human Ubr1 result in the Johanson–Blizzard syndrome characterized by, amongst other phenotypes, frequent mental retardation (Hwang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to work by Hwang et al., 2011.

claim: There are at least three mRNA surveillance pathways: no-go decay (NGD), nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), and non-stop decay (NSD).
source: There are at least three pathways: no-go decay (NGD) targets mRNAs with strong stalls in translation elongation leading to endonucleolytic cleavage of the mRNA, nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) targets messages containing premature termination codons (PTC), and non-stop decay (NSD) targets mRNAs that lack a stop codon.
